title: Τεύχεα ἐκ θαλάμου
titleEn: The Raid on the Armoury — Odyssey 22.101–194
about: Telemachus offers to fetch armour for himself, the swineherd and the cowherd, and Odysseus tells him to hurry while the arrows last. Telemachus brings four shields, eight spears and four helmets from the chamber, and all four arm; Odysseus goes on shooting suitors one by one until the arrows give out, then leans the bow against the doorpost and puts on shield, helmet and spears. He sets Eumaeus to guard the raised door that leads to the passage, the only way out of the hall. Agelaus proposes that someone go up by that door and raise a cry, but the goatherd Melanthius says the passage is too narrow and fetches twelve sets of armour for the suitors by a back way. Odysseus’ heart sinks when he sees them armed; Telemachus admits he left the chamber door ajar, and Eumaeus is sent to shut it. When Melanthius goes back for more, Eumaeus asks whether to kill him or bring him. Odysseus orders him bound and hauled up to the beams, and the two take him as he steps over the threshold with Laertes’ old shield, bind him, and hoist him up. Eumaeus mocks him.

sentences.t:
ὦ πάτερ, ἤδη τοι σάκος οἴσω καὶ δύο δοῦρε
καὶ κυνέην πάγχαλκον, ἐπὶ κροτάφοις ἀραρυῖαν
αὐτός τ’ ἀμφιβαλεῦμαι ἰών, δώσω δὲ συβώτῃ
καὶ τῷ βουκόλῳ ἄλλα·
sentences.l:
“O father, now I will bring you a shield and two spears
and a helmet all of bronze, fitted upon the temples,
and myself I will put it about me as I go, and I will give to the swineherd
and to the cowherd others;
sentences.i: “Father, now I will bring you a shield and two spears and a helmet all of bronze, fitted close to the temples, and I will put my own armour on as I go, and I will give others to the swineherd and the cowherd;
sentences.n: Telemachus is speaking; the line that introduces him closes the previous part. ὦ πάτερ is ‘O father’. σάκος is the great ‘shield’, δοῦρε is the dual of δόρυ ‘spear’ (literally ‘wood’), so ‘two spears’, and δύο makes the number plain. κυνέη is ‘helmet’, here πάγχαλκος ‘all of bronze’. ἀραρυῖαν is the perfect participle of ἀραρίσκω ‘fit’, ‘fitted’, agreeing with the helmet; ἐπὶ κροτάφοις is ‘upon the temples’. τοι is either the enclitic dative ‘to you’ (σοι) or a small particle ‘I tell you’; the English takes it as ‘you’. αὐτός τ’ ἀμφιβαλεῦμαι is ‘and myself I will put (it) about me’, a future middle of ἀμφιβάλλω, with the armour understood; ἰών is ‘going’. δώσω is ‘I will give’, and ἄλλα ‘others’ is neuter plural, the other pieces of armour. συβώτῃ and βουκόλῳ are datives, ‘to the swineherd’ and ‘to the cowherd’.

sentences.t: τετευχῆσθαι γὰρ ἄμεινον.
sentences.l: for to be armed is better.”
sentences.i: for it is better to be armed.”
sentences.n: τετευχῆσθαι is the perfect passive infinitive of τεύχω ‘make, fashion’, ‘to have been equipped’, from the same root as τεύχεα ‘armour’, so ‘to be armed’. ἄμεινον is ‘better’, the neuter comparative of ἀγαθός, with ἐστί left out. γάρ gives the reason for the whole offer.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη πολύμητις Ὀδυσσεύς·
sentences.l: Him answering addressed many-wiled Odysseus:
sentences.i: In answer Odysseus of many wiles said to him:
sentences.n: This is a standing line for an answer. τὸν is the Homeric ‘article’ used as a pronoun, ‘him’; ἀπαμειβόμενος is the participle ‘answering’; προσέφη is ‘addressed’, and πολύμητις ‘many-wiled’ (μῆτις is ‘cunning, craft’) is one of Odysseus’ stock epithets, translated the same way each time. The line occurs again at 170 with the same English.

sentences.t:
οἶσε θέων, ἧός μοι ἀμύνεσθαι πάρ’ ὀϊστοί,
μή μ’ ἀποκινήσωσι θυράων μοῦνον ἐόντα.
sentences.l:
“Bring them, running, while for me there are arrows by me to defend myself with,
lest they dislodge me from the doors, being alone.”
sentences.i: “Run and bring them, while I still have arrows by me to defend myself with, lest they dislodge me from the doors when I am alone.”
sentences.n: οἶσε is the imperative of φέρω ‘bring’, and θέων is the participle ‘running’; the two together give ‘run and bring’. ἧος is the epic ‘while’ (Attic ἕως), μοι is ‘for me’, and πάρ’ is πάρα, ‘are at hand’, so ‘while there are arrows at hand for me’; ἀμύνεσθαι is an infinitive of purpose, ‘to defend myself with’. ὀϊστοί is ‘arrows’. μή with the subjunctive ἀποκινήσωσι gives a fear, ‘lest they dislodge’, and θυράων is the genitive ‘from the doors’, -άων being the old form for -ῶν. μοῦνον ἐόντα is ‘being alone’, in the accusative to agree with μ’, ‘me’.

sentences.t:
ὣς φάτο, Τηλέμαχος δὲ φίλῳ ἐπεπείθετο πατρί,
βῆ δ’ ἴμεναι θάλαμόνδ’, ὅθι οἱ κλυτὰ τεύχεα κεῖτο.
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and Telemachus obeyed his dear father,
and set out to go to the chamber, where his famous armour lay.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and Telemachus obeyed his dear father; he set out for the chamber where the famous armour lay.
sentences.n: φάτο is ‘he spoke’, a past tense without the augment; this first line has been published before and keeps its English. ἐπεπείθετο is the imperfect of ἐπιπείθομαι ‘obey’ with the dative φίλῳ πατρί, ‘his dear father’. βῆ δ’ ἴμεναι is ‘set out to go’, ἴμεναι being the old infinitive (Attic ἰέναι), and θάλαμόνδ’ is ‘to the chamber’, the suffix -δε giving direction. ὅθι is ‘where’, οἱ ‘for him’, and κλυτὰ τεύχεα ‘famous armour’. The verb κεῖτο ‘lay’ is singular although τεύχεα is neuter plural, which Greek allows.

sentences.t:
ἔνθεν τέσσαρα μὲν σάκε’ ἔξελε, δούρατα δ’ ὀκτὼ
καὶ πίσυρας κυνέας χαλκήρεας ἱπποδασείας·
sentences.l:
From there four shields he took out, and spears, eight,
and four helmets, bronze-fitted, horse-haired;
sentences.i: From it he took out four shields, and eight spears, and four bronze-fitted helmets thick with horsehair;
sentences.n: ἔνθεν is ‘from there’, the suffix -θεν giving the place from which. σάκε’ is σάκεα, plural of σάκος ‘shield’; ἔξελε is the aorist of ἐξαιρέω ‘take out’, without the augment. δούρατα is the plural of δόρυ ‘spear’, and ὀκτώ is ‘eight’. πίσυρας is an old form of ‘four’ (τέσσαρας). κυνέας is ‘helmets’, χαλκήρης ‘fitted with bronze’, as in ‘bronze-fitted’ for spears and arrows elsewhere, and ἱπποδάσεια is ‘thick with horsehair’, that is, with a horsehair crest; the three words agree with ‘helmets’. The ano teleia ends the sentence.

sentences.t:
βῆ δὲ φέρων, μάλα δ’ ὦκα φίλον πατέρ’ εἰσαφίκανεν,
αὐτὸς δὲ πρώτιστα περὶ χροῒ δύσετο χαλκόν·
sentences.l:
He set out carrying them, and very swiftly his dear father he reached,
and he himself first of all put the bronze about his body;
sentences.i: He set off carrying them and very quickly reached his dear father, and he himself first of all put the bronze about his body;
sentences.n: βῆ is the unaugmented aorist ‘set out’; φέρων is ‘carrying’, with the armour understood, and μάλα δ’ ὦκα is ‘very swiftly’. εἰσαφίκανεν is the imperfect of εἰσαφικάνω ‘come to, reach’. αὐτὸς δέ is ‘and he himself’, and πρώτιστα ‘first of all’. δύσετο is the aorist middle of δύω; with an object, as here, it means ‘put on’, so ‘put the bronze about his body’, χροΐ being the dative of χρώς ‘skin, body’. ‘The bronze’ stands for the armour.

sentences.t:
ὣς δ’ αὔτως τὼ δμῶε δυέσθην τεύχεα καλά,
ἔσταν δ’ ἀμφ’ Ὀδυσῆα δαΐφρονα ποικιλομήτην.
sentences.l:
So in the same way the two servants put on fine armour,
and stood around Odysseus, wise-minded, of many-colored cunning.
sentences.i: In the same way the two servants put on fine armour, and stood about Odysseus, the wise-hearted, full of shifting cunning.
sentences.n: ὣς δ’ αὔτως is ‘and in the same way’. τὼ δμῶε is the dual ‘the two servants’, the swineherd and the cowherd of 103–104; δυέσθην is a dual past tense of δύω ‘put on’, without the augment. ἔσταν is the old third plural of ἔστην ‘stood’, and ἀμφί with the accusative is ‘around’. Ὀδυσῆα is the same name as Ὀδυσσῆα elsewhere in the part, with one σ fewer. δαΐφρων is a stock epithet whose sense is doubtful: it is read from δαῆναι ‘to learn, know’, so ‘wise-minded’, but ancient scholars also took it from δαΐ ‘in battle’, ‘warlike-minded’; the English follows the first. ποικιλομήτης is ‘of many-colored (shifting) cunning’, ποικίλος ‘many-coloured’ and μῆτις ‘cunning’.

sentences.t: αὐτὰρ ὅ γ’, ὄφρα μὲν αὐτῷ ἀμύνεσθαι ἔσαν ἰοί.
sentences.l: But he, as long as for himself to defend there were arrows,
sentences.i: But he, for as long as he had arrows to defend himself with,
sentences.n: Murray begins a paragraph here. αὐτὰρ ὅ γ’ is ‘but he’, ὅ being the pronoun. ὄφρα is ‘as long as’, and it is answered by τόφρα ‘for so long’ at the start of the next line. ἔσαν is ‘were’ (Attic ἦσαν), αὐτῷ is ‘for himself’, and ἀμύνεσθαι is an infinitive of purpose, ‘to defend’. ἰοί is ‘arrows’, plural of ἰός. Murray’s full stop falls here, so this unit hangs on the next: the English leaves it open.

sentences.t:
τόφρα μνηστήρων ἕνα γ’ αἰεὶ ᾧ ἐνὶ οἴκῳ
βάλλε τιτυσκόμενος·
sentences.l:
for so long, of the suitors, always one at a time, in his own house,
he kept hitting, taking aim;
sentences.i: for so long he kept hitting the suitors one at a time in his own house, taking aim at each;
sentences.n: μνηστήρων is the genitive ‘of the suitors’, and ἕνα γ’ αἰεί is ‘one each time’: ἕνα is ‘one’, αἰεί ‘always’, the γε a small emphasis. ᾧ ἐνὶ οἴκῳ is ‘in his own house’, with ἐνί placed between the possessive ὅς (here ‘his own’, not the relative) and its noun. βάλλε is the imperfect ‘kept hitting, shooting at’, and τιτυσκόμενος is ‘taking aim’. This unit is the answer to ὄφρα in the line before.

sentences.t: τοὶ δ’ ἀγχιστῖνοι ἔπιπτον.
sentences.l: and they, in close succession, fell.
sentences.i: and they fell one close upon another.
sentences.n: τοί is the old form of the plural ‘they’. ἔπιπτον is the imperfect of πίπτω ‘fall’. ἀγχιστῖνοι is a rare word: it is built on ἄγχι ‘near’, and ‘close together, in close succession’ is the sense the context gives, but the exact meaning is not known.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ λίπον ἰοὶ ὀϊστεύοντα ἄνακτα,
τόξον μὲν πρὸς σταθμὸν ἐϋσταθέος μεγάροιο
ἔκλιν’ ἑστάμεναι, πρὸς ἐνώπια παμφανόωντα,
sentences.l:
But when the arrows left the lord as he shot,
the bow against the doorpost of the well-founded hall
he leaned to stand, against the shining inner walls,
sentences.i: But when the arrows failed the lord as he shot, he leaned the bow against the doorpost of the well-founded hall, to stand there against the shining inner walls,
sentences.n: λίπον is ‘left, failed’, with ἰοί ‘arrows’ as subject and ὀϊστεύοντα ἄνακτα, ‘the lord as he shot’, as object; ἄναξ is ‘lord’, here Odysseus in his own hall. σταθμός is ‘doorpost’, and ἐϋσταθέος μεγάροιο ‘of the well-founded hall’, ἐϋσταθής meaning ‘firmly standing’. ἔκλιν’ is ἔκλινε, ‘leaned’, and ἑστάμεναι is the infinitive ‘to stand’, in the sense ‘so that it stood’. ἐνώπια are the faces of the walls looking inward, and παμφανόωντα is ‘shining’ (literally ‘all-shining’). The sentence runs on to line 125, so the unit is cut at the comma.

sentences.t:
αὐτὸς δ’ ἀμφ’ ὤμοισι σάκος θέτο τετραθέλυμνον,
κρατὶ δ’ ἐπ’ ἰφθίμῳ κυνέην εὔτυκτον ἔθηκεν,
ἵππουριν, δεινὸν δὲ λόφος καθύπερθεν ἔνευεν·
sentences.i: and he set the four-layered shield about his own shoulders, and on his mighty head he placed the well-made helmet, with its horsetail plume, and fearsomely the crest nodded above;
sentences.n: θέτο is the aorist middle of τίθημι, without the augment, ‘put for himself’. τετραθέλυμνον is ‘of four layers’, but θέλυμνα is an obscure word (‘layers’ or ‘foundations’), so ‘four-layered’ is the usual guess and the exact meaning is not known. κρατί is the dative of κάρη ‘head’, ἰφθίμῳ ‘mighty’, κυνέην εὔτυκτον ‘well-made helmet’, and ἔθηκεν the aorist ‘placed’. ἵππουριν is ‘with a horse’s tail’, that is, a horsehair plume, and λόφος is the ‘crest’; ἔνευεν is ‘nodded’, imperfect, and καθύπερθεν ‘from above’. The ano teleia after ἔνευεν ends the unit.

sentences.t: εἵλετο δ’ ἄλκιμα δοῦρε δύω κεκορυθμένα χαλκῷ.
sentences.l: and he took two sturdy spears, armed with bronze.
sentences.i: and he took two sturdy spears, armed with bronze.
sentences.n: εἵλετο δ’ begins a new sentence after the ano teleia at the end of 124. ἄλκιμα is ‘sturdy’, as with a spear elsewhere, and δοῦρε δύω is dual and number, ‘two spears’. κεκορυθμένα, from κόρυς ‘helmet’, means literally ‘helmeted’, so ‘armed’ with bronze; it agrees with the spears.

sentences.t:
ὀρσοθύρη δέ τις ἔσκεν ἐϋδμήτῳ ἐνὶ τοίχῳ,
ἀκρότατον δὲ παρ’ οὐδὸν ἐϋσταθέος μεγάροιο
ἦν ὁδὸς ἐς λαύρην, σανίδες δ’ ἔχον εὖ ἀραρυῖαι.
sentences.l:
Now there was a raised door in the well-built wall,
and by the topmost threshold of the well-founded hall
there was a way into the passage, and boards held it, well fitted.
sentences.i: There was a raised door in the well-built wall, and beside the topmost threshold of the well-founded hall there was a way into the passage, which well-fitted boards closed off.
sentences.n: Murray begins a paragraph here. ὀρσοθύρη is a compound whose first part is not certain; ‘raised door’ is the traditional sense, a door set up above floor level, and what kind of opening it was is not known. ἔσκεν is simply ‘there was’ (ἦν), and ἐϋδμήτῳ ‘well-built’ goes with τοίχῳ ‘wall’. οὐδός is ‘threshold’ and ἀκρότατον ‘topmost’; the exact point meant is not clear. λαύρη is a ‘passage, lane’, ἐς λαύρην ‘into the passage’. σανίδες are ‘boards’, probably door-leaves, though the Greek does not say; ἔχον is ‘held’, the object being the opening, and ἀραρυῖαι, again from ἀραρίσκω, is ‘fitted’, here feminine plural.

sentences.t:
τὴν δ’ Ὀδυσεὺς φράζεσθαι ἀνώγει δῖον ὑφορβὸν
ἑσταότ’ ἄγχ’ αὐτῆς·
sentences.l:
And this Odysseus bade the heavenly swineherd to watch,
standing close by it;
sentences.i: Odysseus told the heavenly swineherd to keep watch on it, standing close beside it;
sentences.n: τὴν is ‘it’, that is the raised door. φράζεσθαι is ‘to take note of, watch’, and ἀνώγει ‘bade’. δῖον ὑφορβόν is ‘the heavenly swineherd’: δῖος is the stock epithet, translated ‘heavenly’, and ὑφορβός is ‘swineherd’. ἑσταότ’ is the perfect participle of ἵστημι, ‘standing’, accusative to agree with the swineherd. The ano teleia after αὐτῆς, in the middle of line 130, ends the unit.

sentences.t: μία δ’ οἴη γίγνετ’ ἐφορμή.
sentences.l: and only one was the way of attack.
sentences.i: for there was only one way to attack from.
sentences.n: μία δ’ οἴη is ‘one only’, and ἐφορμή, from ἐπί and ὁρμή, is ‘a rush upon, a point of attack’. γίγνετ’ is γίγνετο, the imperfect, ‘was’. The clause gives the reason for standing guard at the door of 126.

sentences.t: τοῖς δ’ Ἀγέλεως μετέειπεν, ἔπος πάντεσσι πιφαύσκων·
sentences.l: And among them Agelaus spoke, making known a word to all:
sentences.i: Then Agelaus spoke among them, making his word known to all:
sentences.n: τοῖς is ‘among them’, the suitors. Ἀγέλεως is Ionic for Ἀγέλαος, Agelaus; the vocative Ἀγέλαε is in line 136. μετέειπεν is ‘spoke among’ with the uncontracted ending, and πιφαύσκων is a participle ‘making known, declaring’, with ἔπος ‘a word’ and πάντεσσι ‘to all’, the -εσσι dative.

sentences.t:
ὦ φίλοι, οὐκ ἂν δή τις ἀν’ ὀρσοθύρην ἀναβαίη
καὶ εἴποι λαοῖσι, βοὴ δ’ ὤκιστα γένοιτο;
sentences.l:
“O friends, would not someone go up by the raised door
and tell the people, and a shout most swiftly come about?
sentences.i: “Friends, could not someone go up through the raised door and tell the people, and a cry arise as quickly as possible?
sentences.n: ὦ φίλοι is ‘O friends’. οὐκ ἂν ... ἀναβαίη is a negative question with the optative and ἄν, ‘would not someone go up?’, a way of proposing it. ἀν’ is ἀνά ‘up by’ with the accusative ὀρσοθύρην. εἴποι is the aorist optative ‘tell’, and λαοῖσι the dative ‘the people’. βοή is ‘shout, cry’, and ὤκιστα, the superlative of ὠκύς, is ‘most swiftly’, so ‘as quickly as possible’. The Greek question mark is the semicolon.

sentences.t: τῷ κε τάχ’ οὗτος ἀνὴρ νῦν ὕστατα τοξάσσαιτο.
sentences.l: then soon this man now for the last time would shoot.”
sentences.i: and then this man would soon be shooting for the last time.”
sentences.n: τῷ is ‘then, in that case’. κε is ἄν, so κε ... τοξάσσαιτο is ‘would shoot’, the optative of τοξάζομαι ‘shoot with the bow’. τάχα is ‘soon’ and ὕστατα ‘for the last time’. The line repeats one from the previous part and has the same English. The speech ends here.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπε Μελάνθιος, αἰπόλος αἰγῶν·
sentences.l: Him then in turn addressed Melanthius, the goatherd of goats:
sentences.i: Then Melanthius, the goatherd of the goats, spoke to him in turn:
sentences.n: Murray begins a paragraph here. This is a standing reply line: τὸν is ‘him’, αὖτε ‘in turn’, and προσέειπε ‘addressed’. αἰπόλος is ‘goatherd’ and αἰγῶν the genitive plural of αἴξ ‘goat’, so ‘goatherd of the goats’; the line has been published before and has the same English.

sentences.t: οὔ πως ἔστ’, Ἀγέλαε διοτρεφές·
sentences.l: “In no way is it possible, Agelaus, Zeus-nurtured one;
sentences.i: “It cannot be done, Agelaus, Zeus-nurtured one;
sentences.n: οὔ πως ἔστ’ is ‘in no way is it possible’; ἔστι with the accent on the first syllable means ‘it is possible’. Ἀγέλαε is the vocative of Agelaus, and διοτρεφές, a stock epithet meaning ‘Zeus-nurtured’, is its vocative too.

sentences.t:
ἄγχι γὰρ αἰνῶς
αὐλῆς καλὰ θύρετρα καὶ ἀργαλέον στόμα λαύρης·
sentences.l:
for terribly near
are the court’s fair doors, and grievous is the mouth of the passage;
sentences.i: for the fair doors of the court are terribly close, and the mouth of the passage is grievous;
sentences.n: ἄγχι is ‘near’, αἰνῶς ‘terribly’, and γάρ ‘for’. αὐλῆς is the genitive of αὐλή ‘courtyard’, θύρετρα ‘doors, doorways’, neuter plural, with καλά ‘fair’. ἀργαλέον is ‘grievous’, in the sense of hard to deal with, and στόμα λαύρης is ‘the mouth of the passage’. The Greek does not say what the doors are near; the picture is of the way out through the passage of 128. The ano teleia ends the unit.

sentences.t: καί χ’ εἷς πάντας ἐρύκοι ἀνήρ, ὅς τ’ ἄλκιμος εἴη.
sentences.l: and one man could hold back all, if he were valiant.
sentences.i: and a single man could hold them all back, if he were valiant.
sentences.n: καί χ’ is καί κε. εἷς ‘one’ here is the number, not an article. ἐρύκοι is the optative ‘would hold back’, and with κε it states what could happen. πάντας is ‘all’. ὅς τ’ ἄλκιμος εἴη is ‘who would be valiant’, the optative εἴη matching ἐρύκοι and the epic τε adding a general sense, so ‘if he were valiant’ is the force; ἄλκιμος, ‘valiant’, is built on ἀλκή ‘fighting strength’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἄγεθ’, ὑμῖν τεύχε’ ἐνείκω θωρηχθῆναι
ἐκ θαλάμου·
sentences.l:
But come, let me bring you armour, for you to arm yourselves,
from the chamber;
sentences.i: But come, let me bring you armour from the chamber, for you to arm yourselves with;
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἄγεθ’ is ‘but come’, ἄγεθ’ being ἄγετε. ἐνείκω is the aorist subjunctive ‘let me bring’, a request to be allowed, with ὑμῖν ‘for you’ and τεύχε’ (τεύχεα) ‘armour’. θωρηχθῆναι is the aorist passive infinitive of θωρήσσω ‘arm’, ‘to be armed’, giving the purpose. ἐκ θαλάμου is ‘from the chamber’. The ano teleia falls in the middle of line 140.

sentences.t:
ἔνδον γάρ, ὀΐομαι, οὐδέ πη ἄλλῃ
τεύχεα κατθέσθην Ὀδυσεὺς καὶ φαίδιμος υἱός.
sentences.l:
for within, I suppose, and nowhere else
Odysseus and his glorious son put away the armour.”
sentences.i: for I suppose it is inside, and nowhere else, that Odysseus and his glorious son put the armour away.”
sentences.n: ἔνδον is ‘within’. ὀΐομαι is ‘I suppose, I suspect’, parenthetical. οὐδέ πη ἄλλῃ is ‘nor anywhere else’. κατθέσθην is a dual, the aorist middle of κατατίθημι ‘put away, lay down’, because the subjects are two, Ὀδυσσεύς and φαίδιμος υἱός. φαίδιμος is ‘glorious’. The speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ὣς εἰπὼν ἀνέβαινε Μελάνθιος, αἰπόλος αἰγῶν,
εἰς θαλάμους Ὀδυσῆος ἀνὰ ῥῶγας μεγάροιο.
sentences.l:
So saying, up went Melanthius, the goatherd of goats,
into the chambers of Odysseus, up through the clefts of the hall.
sentences.i: So saying, Melanthius, the goatherd of the goats, went up into the chambers of Odysseus, through the clefts of the hall.
sentences.n: Murray begins a paragraph here. ὣς εἰπών is ‘so saying’, the aorist participle; ἀνέβαινε is the imperfect ‘was going up’. θαλάμους is ‘chambers’, and Ὀδυσῆος the genitive of Ὀδυσεύς. ἀνά with the accusative is ‘up along, through’. ῥῶγας is accusative plural of ῥώξ, which means ‘cleft, chink’; what part of the hall is meant is not known, and ‘clefts’ keeps the word.

sentences.t:
ἔνθεν δώδεκα μὲν σάκε’ ἔξελε, τόσσα δὲ δοῦρα
καὶ τόσσας κυνέας χαλκήρεας ἱπποδασείας·
sentences.l:
From there twelve shields he took out, and as many spears,
and as many helmets, bronze-fitted, horse-haired;
sentences.i: From it he took out twelve shields, and as many spears, and as many bronze-fitted helmets thick with horsehair;
sentences.n: The line is built like 110–111, with δώδεκα ‘twelve’ for ‘four’ and ‘eight’, and τόσσα, τόσσας ‘so many’, giving ‘as many’ spears and helmets. The words for shield, spear and helmet are the same as there, and ‘bronze-fitted’ and ‘thick with horsehair’ are repeated each time.

sentences.t: βῆ δ’ ἴμεναι, μάλα δ’ ὦκα φέρων μνηστῆρσιν ἔδωκεν.
sentences.l: He set out to go, and very swiftly, carrying them, gave them to the suitors.
sentences.i: He set off, and very quickly carried the armour away and gave it to the suitors.
sentences.n: βῆ δ’ ἴμεναι is ‘set out to go’, as in line 109, and μάλα δ’ ὦκα ‘very swiftly’ and φέρων ‘carrying’ as in line 112. μνηστῆρσιν is the dative plural ‘to the suitors’, and ἔδωκεν the aorist ‘gave’.

sentences.t:
καὶ τότ’ Ὀδυσσῆος λύτο γούνατα καὶ φίλον ἦτορ,
ὡς περιβαλλομένους ἴδε τεύχεα χερσί τε δοῦρα
μακρὰ τινάσσοντας·
sentences.i: And then Odysseus’ knees gave way, and his heart too, when he saw them putting on armour and brandishing long spears in their hands;
sentences.n: λύτο is ‘were loosed’, the aorist middle (passive in sense) of λύω without the augment; ‘the knees and heart were loosed’ is an idiom for losing strength and courage. γούνατα is plural of γόνυ ‘knee’, and φίλον ἦτορ is ‘his dear heart’, φίλον acting almost as ‘his own’. The first line has been published before and keeps its English. ὡς here is ‘when’. περιβαλλομένους is the middle participle ‘putting about themselves’, with τεύχεα ‘armour’ as object, and τινάσσοντας ‘brandishing’ goes with δοῦρα μακρά, ‘long spears’. The ano teleia falls in the middle of line 149.

sentences.t: μέγα δ’ αὐτῷ φαίνετο ἔργον.
sentences.l: and great to him appeared the task.
sentences.i: and the task before him seemed a great one.
sentences.n: μέγα ... ἔργον is ‘a great task’, and αὐτῷ the dative ‘to him’, a plain pronoun, not ‘himself’. φαίνετο is ‘appeared’. The sentence is short and flat after the long description of the arming.

sentences.t: αἶψα δὲ Τηλέμαχον ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα·
sentences.l: And at once, to Telemachus, winged words he spoke:
sentences.i: At once he spoke winged words to Telemachus:
sentences.n: αἶψα is ‘at once’. ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα is the standing line-ending ‘spoke winged words’: ἔπεα is ‘words’, πτερόεντα ‘winged’ (from πτερόν), προσηύδα ‘spoke to’, with Τηλέμαχον the accusative of the person addressed. The line has been published before and has the same English.

sentences.t:
Τηλέμαχ’, ἦ μάλα δή τις ἐνὶ μεγάροισι γυναικῶν
νῶϊν ἐποτρύνει πόλεμον κακὸν ἠὲ Μελανθεύς.
sentences.l:
“Telemachus, surely indeed some one of the women in the halls
is stirring up for us two an evil war, or else Melantheus.”
sentences.i: “Telemachus, surely one of the women in the halls is stirring up an evil fight against us, or else it is Melanthius.”
sentences.n: Murray begins a paragraph here. The vocative Τηλέμαχ’ is elided. ἦ μάλα δή is ‘surely indeed’, and τις ... γυναικῶν ‘some one of the women’, a partitive genitive. ἐποτρύνει is ‘stirs up’, νῶϊν the dual dative ‘for us two’, and πόλεμον κακόν ‘an evil war’. ἠέ is ‘or’. Μελανθεύς is a second form of the name Μελάνθιος and is the same man, the goatherd; in 159 he is ‘the son of Dolius’.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖ Τηλέμαχος πεπνυμένος ἀντίον ηὔδα·
sentences.l: To him in turn prudent Telemachus spoke, face to face:
sentences.i: Then prudent Telemachus spoke to him in turn, face to face:
sentences.n: Murray begins a paragraph here. This is a standing reply line: τὸν is ‘him’, αὖ ‘in turn’, πεπνυμένος ‘prudent’, a stock epithet of Telemachus, and ἀντίον ηὔδα ‘spoke face to face’. The line has been published before and has the same English.

sentences.t:
ὦ πάτερ, αὐτὸς ἐγὼ τόδε γ’ ἤμβροτον—οὐδέ τις ἄλλος
αἴτιος—ὃς θαλάμοιο θύρην πυκινῶς ἀραρυῖαν
κάλλιπον ἀγκλίνας·
sentences.i: “Father, it was I myself who made this mistake—and no one else is to blame—I who left the tightly fitted door of the chamber ajar;
sentences.n: ἤμβροτον is the aorist of ἁμαρτάνω ‘miss, err’, ‘I made a mistake’; τόδε is ‘in this’, an accusative of respect. The clause οὐδέ τις ἄλλος αἴτιος is ‘and no one else (is) to blame’, with ἐστί left out, set between dashes. ὅς ... κάλλιπον is ‘I who left’: the relative takes the person of the verb, as ἐγώ is its antecedent. κάλλιπον is κατέλιπον with the κατά shortened and assimilated. θαλάμοιο is the genitive ‘of the chamber’, πυκινῶς ‘tightly’, and ἀραρυῖαν ‘fitted’, agreeing with θύρην ‘door’. ἀγκλίνας is ‘having leaned back’, that is, left it ajar, from ἀνακλίνω with ν assimilated. The ano teleia after ἀγκλίνας, in the middle of line 156, ends the unit.

sentences.t: τῶν δὲ σκοπὸς ἦεν ἀμείνων.
sentences.l: but their watcher was better.
sentences.i: but their lookout was the better one.
sentences.n: τῶν is ‘their’, and σκοπός ‘watcher, lookout’; ἦεν is ‘was’ and ἀμείνων ‘better’, the comparative of ἀγαθός. The speech ends only at 159.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἴθι, δῖ’ Εὔμαιε, θύρην ἐπίθες θαλάμοιο
καὶ φράσαι ἤ τις ἄρ’ ἐστὶ γυναικῶν ἣ τάδε ῥέζει,
ἢ υἱὸς Δολίοιο, Μελανθεύς, τόν περ ὀΐω.
sentences.l:
But go, heavenly Eumaeus, put to the door of the chamber
and see whether it is some one of the women who does these things,
or the son of Dolius, Melantheus, whom indeed I suspect.”
sentences.i: But go, heavenly Eumaeus, shut the door of the chamber and see whether it is one of the women who is doing this, or Melanthius, the son of Dolius, whom I do suspect.”
sentences.n: ἴθι is the imperative of εἶμι ‘go’. δῖ’ Εὔμαιε is the vocative of δῖος with its ending elided, ‘heavenly Eumaeus’, the same epithet as in ‘heavenly swineherd’. ἐπίθες is the aorist imperative ‘put to’, that is, shut. φράσαι is ‘observe, see’, and ἤ ... ἢ ... is ‘whether ... or’. ῥέζει is ‘does’. Δολίοιο is the genitive of Δολίος, Dolius. Μελανθεύς is again the second form of Melanthius. τόν περ ὀΐω is ‘whom indeed I suspect’; ὀΐω is the first person singular, and here ‘suspect’, as in the form ὀϊόμεθ’ in 165. The speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ὣς οἱ μὲν τοιαῦτα πρὸς ἀλλήλους ἀγόρευον,
βῆ δ’ αὖτις θάλαμόνδε Μελάνθιος, αἰπόλος αἰγῶν,
οἴσων τεύχεα καλά.
sentences.l:
So they, such things to one another were saying,
and again to the chamber went Melanthius, the goatherd of goats,
to bring fine armour.
sentences.i: So they talked in this way with one another, and Melanthius, the goatherd of the goats, went again to the chamber to bring fine armour.
sentences.n: Murray begins a paragraph here. ὣς οἱ μὲν ... ἀγόρευον is ‘so they were saying’; οἱ is the pronoun ‘they’, and the first line has been published before and keeps its English. αὖτις is ‘again’, and βῆ ... θάλαμόνδε ‘went to the chamber’. οἴσων is the future participle of φέρω, ‘to bring’, expressing purpose. τεύχεα καλά is ‘fine armour’. The full stop falls in the middle of line 162.

sentences.t:
νόησε δὲ δῖος ὑφορβός,
αἶψα δ’ Ὀδυσσῆα προσεφώνεεν ἐγγὺς ἐόντα·
sentences.l:
and he noticed it, the heavenly swineherd,
and at once spoke to Odysseus, who was near:
sentences.i: and the heavenly swineherd noticed it, and at once spoke to Odysseus, who was near him:
sentences.n: νόησε is the aorist ‘noticed, perceived’, from νοέω; the object, Melanthius going, is understood. δῖος ὑφορβός is ‘the heavenly swineherd’. προσεφώνεεν is ‘spoke to’, the imperfect with the uncontracted ending, and ἐγγὺς ἐόντα is ‘who was near’, accusative agreeing with Ὀδυσσῆα. The ano teleia introduces his speech.

sentences.t:
διογενὲς Λαερτιάδη, πολυμήχαν’ Ὀδυσσεῦ,
κεῖνος δ’ αὖτ’ ἀΐδηλος ἀνήρ, ὃν ὀϊόμεθ’ αὐτοί,
ἔρχεται ἐς θάλαμον·
sentences.i: “Zeus-born son of Laertes, Odysseus, man of many devices, that ruinous man, the one we ourselves suspect, is going again to the chamber;
sentences.n: Murray begins a paragraph here. The first line is a standing address to Odysseus and keeps the English it has had where it appeared before: διογενές ‘Zeus-sprung’, Λαερτιάδη ‘son of Laertes’, πολυμήχανος ‘many-devising’. κεῖνος is ἐκεῖνος, ‘that’, and αὖτ’ is αὖτε ‘again’. ἀΐδηλος is a difficult word: it is taken either as ‘destroying’ or as ‘unseen’, and ‘ruinous’ follows the first. ὃν ὀϊόμεθ’ αὐτοί is ‘whom we ourselves suspect’, ὀϊόμεθα being the present ‘we suspect’ and αὐτοί ‘ourselves’. ἔρχεται is ‘is going’. The ano teleia falls in the middle of line 166.

sentences.t:
σὺ δέ μοι νημερτὲς ἐνίσπες,
ἤ μιν ἀποκτείνω, αἴ κε κρείσσων γε γένωμαι,
ἦε σοὶ ἐνθάδ’ ἄγω, ἵν’ ὑπερβασίας ἀποτίσῃ
πολλάς, ὅσσας οὗτος ἐμήσατο σῷ ἐνὶ οἴκῳ.
sentences.l:
and you, tell me unerringly,
whether I am to kill him, if I prove the stronger,
or bring him here to you, so that he may pay for oversteppings,
many, as many as this man devised in your house.”
sentences.i: but you, tell me unerringly whether I am to kill him, if I prove the stronger, or bring him here to you, so that he may pay for the many transgressions that this man devised in your house.”
sentences.n: ἐνίσπες is the aorist imperative ‘tell’, and νημερτές ‘unerringly’ is an adverb from the adjective for ‘unerring’; μοι is ‘to me’. ἤ ... ἦε is ‘whether ... or’, with a subjunctive for each of the two things he asks, ἀποκτείνω ‘am I to kill’ and ἄγω ‘am I to bring’. αἴ κε is εἰ ἄν ‘if’, and κρείσσων ‘stronger’. μιν is ‘him’, σοί ‘to you’, ἐνθάδ’ ‘here’. ἵνα is ‘so that’, ἀποτίσῃ is ‘may pay back’, and ὑπερβασίας is ‘transgressions’, from ὑπερβαίνω ‘step over’. ὅσσας is ‘as many as’, ἐμήσατο ‘devised’, and σῷ ἐνὶ οἴκῳ ‘in your house’. The speech ends here.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη πολύμητις Ὀδυσσεύς·
sentences.l: Him answering addressed many-wiled Odysseus:
sentences.i: In answer Odysseus of many wiles said to him:
sentences.n: Murray begins a paragraph here. This is the same line as 105 and has the same English.

sentences.t:
ἦ τοι ἐγὼ καὶ Τηλέμαχος μνηστῆρας ἀγαυοὺς
σχήσομεν ἔντοσθεν μεγάρων, μάλα περ μεμαῶτας.
sentences.l:
“Truly I and Telemachus the noble suitors
will hold back within the halls, though they are very eager.
sentences.i: “I and Telemachus will hold the noble suitors back inside the halls, however eager they are.
sentences.n: ἦ τοι is ‘truly’. ἐγὼ καὶ Τηλέμαχος is ‘I and Telemachus’, the subject of the first person plural σχήσομεν, the future of ἔχω, ‘we will hold back’. μνηστῆρας ἀγαυούς is ‘the noble suitors’, ἀγαυός being ‘noble’. ἔντοσθεν is ‘inside’, with the genitive μεγάρων. μάλα περ μεμαῶτας is ‘though very eager’: μεμαῶτας is the perfect participle of μαίομαι ‘strive, be eager’, and περ makes it concessive.

sentences.t:
σφῶϊ δ’ ἀποστρέψαντε πόδας καὶ χεῖρας ὕπερθεν
ἐς θάλαμον βαλέειν, σανίδας δ’ ἐκδῆσαι ὄπισθε,
sentences.l:
But you two, having twisted back his feet and hands above,
are to throw him into the chamber, and to tie boards on behind,
sentences.i: But you two are to twist his feet and hands back over him, throw him into the chamber, and fasten boards on behind,
sentences.n: σφῶϊ is the dual ‘you two’, and ἀποστρέψαντε the dual aorist participle ‘having twisted back’; πόδας καὶ χεῖρας is ‘feet and hands’, and ὕπερθεν ‘above, over’, probably over his back. βαλέειν and ἐκδῆσαι are infinitives used as commands, ‘are to throw’ and ‘are to tie’, with μιν ‘him’ understood. ἐς θάλαμον is ‘into the chamber’. σανίδας δ’ ἐκδῆσαι ὄπισθε is ‘and to tie boards on behind’; what is meant, whether boards lashed to his back or a plank he is bound to, is not clear from the words. The sentence is long, and the comma here is where it pauses most.

sentences.t:
σειρὴν δὲ πλεκτὴν ἐξ αὐτοῦ πειρήναντε
κίον’ ἀν’ ὑψηλὴν ἐρύσαι πελάσαι τε δοκοῖσιν,
ὥς κεν δηθὰ ζωὸς ἐὼν χαλέπ’ ἄλγεα πάσχῃ·
sentences.l:
and a plaited rope, from him having fastened it,
up the high pillar to haul and to bring near the beams,
so that for long, alive, he may suffer harsh pains.”
sentences.i: and fasten a plaited rope to him, haul him up the high pillar and bring him close to the beams, so that he may suffer harsh pains for a long time, alive.”
sentences.n: σειρὴν πλεκτήν is ‘a plaited rope’. πειρήναντε is the dual aorist participle ‘having fastened’, with ἐξ αὐτοῦ ‘from him’, that is, attached to him. κίον’ is κίονα ‘pillar’, ἀν’ is ἀνά ‘up along’, and ὑψηλήν ‘high’. ἐρύσαι and πελάσαι are aorist infinitives, again used as commands, ‘to haul’ and ‘to bring near’, and δοκοῖσιν is the dative ‘to the beams’. ὥς κεν with the subjunctive πάσχῃ is ‘so that he may suffer’. δηθά is ‘for a long time’, ζωὸς ἐών ‘being alive’, and χαλεπά ‘harsh’ goes with ἄλγεα ‘pains’. The speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἔφαθ’, οἱ δ’ ἄρα τοῦ μάλα μὲν κλύον ἠδ’ ἐπίθοντο,
βὰν δ’ ἴμεν ἐς θάλαμον, λαθέτην δέ μιν ἔνδον ἐόντα.
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and they then readily heard him and obeyed,
and set out to go to the chamber, and escaped his notice as he was within.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and they listened to him readily and obeyed, and went to the chamber, and escaped his notice while he was inside.
sentences.n: Murray begins a paragraph here. The first line has been published before and keeps its English. ἔφαθ’ is ἔφατο ‘he spoke’, and οἱ δ’ ἄρα is ‘and they then’. τοῦ is ‘him’, with κλύον ‘heard’, which takes the genitive of the person; ἐπίθοντο is ‘obeyed’. βὰν is ‘they set out’, an aorist without the augment, and ἴμεν is ‘to go’. λαθέτην is the dual aorist of λανθάνω ‘escape the notice of’, so the two of them; its object μιν is ‘him’, and ἔνδον ἐόντα ‘being inside’ agrees with it.

sentences.t:
ἦ τοι ὁ μὲν θαλάμοιο μυχὸν κάτα τεύχε’ ἐρεύνα,
τὼ δ’ ἔσταν ἑκάτερθε παρὰ σταθμοῖσι μένοντε.
sentences.l:
Now he indeed down in the recess of the chamber was searching for armour,
and the two stood on either side by the doorposts, waiting.
sentences.i: Now he was searching for armour in the innermost part of the chamber, while the two stood on either side by the doorposts, waiting.
sentences.n: ἦ τοι is ‘now indeed’. ὁ μέν is ‘he’ and τὼ δέ ‘the two’, so the clauses answer each other. μυχόν is the ‘innermost part, recess’, and κάτα is κατά placed after its noun, ‘down in’. ἐρεύνα is the imperfect of ἐρευνάω ‘search’. ἔσταν is the aorist ‘stood’. ἑκάτερθε is ‘on either side’, and σταθμοῖσι the dative plural of σταθμός ‘doorpost’; μένοντε is the dual participle ‘waiting’.

sentences.t:
εὖθ’ ὑπὲρ οὐδὸν ἔβαινε Μελάνθιος, αἰπόλος αἰγῶν,
τῇ ἑτέρῃ μὲν χειρὶ φέρων καλὴν τρυφάλειαν,
τῇ δ’ ἑτέρῃ σάκος εὐρὺ γέρον, πεπαλαγμένον ἄζῃ,
Λαέρτεω ἥρωος, ὃ κουρίζων φορέεσκε·
sentences.l:
When over the threshold stepped Melanthius, the goatherd of goats,
in the one hand carrying a fine helm,
and in the other a broad old shield, spattered with grime,
of the hero Laertes, which as a youth he used to carry;
sentences.i: Just as Melanthius, the goatherd of the goats, was stepping over the threshold, carrying a fine helmet in one hand and in the other a broad old shield, spattered with grime, that had belonged to the hero Laertes and that he used to carry when he was young;
sentences.n: εὖθ’ is ‘when’. ἔβαινε is the imperfect ‘was stepping’, ὑπὲρ οὐδόν ‘over the threshold’. τῇ ἑτέρῃ μὲν χειρί ... τῇ δ’ ἑτέρῃ is ‘in the one hand ... in the other’. τρυφάλεια is a kind of helmet, and its derivation is not known. σάκος εὐρύ is ‘a broad shield’; γέρον, ‘old’, is the neuter of γέρων ‘old man’, a word for a person, here said of the shield that was a man’s. πεπαλαγμένον is the perfect passive participle of παλάσσω ‘spatter’, and ἄζῃ the dative ‘with grime, dry dirt’. Λαέρτεω is the genitive of Λαέρτης, with the old ending -εω, and ἥρωος is ‘of the hero’. ὃ κουρίζων φορέεσκε is ‘which he used to carry as a youth’: κουρίζων is ‘being a young man’, φορέεσκε an iterative imperfect, and the subject is Laertes.

sentences.t: δὴ τότε γ’ ἤδη κεῖτο, ῥαφαὶ δὲ λέλυντο ἱμάντων·
sentences.l: then indeed already it lay, and the seams of the straps were undone;
sentences.i: By now it simply lay there, and the stitching of the straps had come undone;
sentences.n: δὴ τότε γ’ ἤδη is ‘by then already’. κεῖτο is ‘lay’, imperfect, and the shield is the subject. ῥαφαί are ‘seams, stitches’, and ἱμάντων is the genitive ‘of the straps’. λέλυντο is the pluperfect passive of λύω, ‘had been loosed’.

sentences.t:
τὼ δ’ ἄρ’ ἐπαΐξανθ’ ἑλέτην ἔρυσάν τέ μιν εἴσω
κουρίξ, ἐν δαπέδῳ δὲ χαμαὶ βάλον ἀχνύμενον κῆρ,
sentences.l:
and the two then, rushing upon him, seized him and dragged him inside
by the hair, and on the floor on the ground threw him, grieving in heart,
sentences.i: The two sprang on him, seized him and dragged him inside by the hair, and threw him down on the floor, grieving in his heart,
sentences.n: τὼ δ’ ἄρ’ is ‘and the two then’. ἐπαΐξανθ’ is the dual aorist participle ‘rushing upon’, and ἑλέτην the dual aorist of αἱρέω ‘seized’. ἔρυσαν is a plural ‘dragged’, and the Greek mixes dual and plural freely for the same two men. μιν is ‘him’, εἴσω ‘inside’, and κουρίξ ‘by the hair’. ἐν δαπέδῳ ... χαμαί is ‘on the floor, on the ground’, the two saying much the same thing. βάλον is ‘threw’, an unaugmented aorist. ἀχνύμενον κῆρ is ‘grieving in heart’, κῆρ being an accusative of respect.

sentences.t:
σὺν δὲ πόδας χεῖράς τε δέον θυμαλγέϊ δεσμῷ
εὖ μάλ’ ἀποστρέψαντε διαμπερές, ὡς ἐκέλευσεν
υἱὸς Λαέρταο, πολύτλας δῖος Ὀδυσσεύς·
sentences.i: and bound his feet and hands together with a bond that grieved the heart, twisting them back very thoroughly, as the son of Laertes, much-enduring, heavenly Odysseus, had ordered;
sentences.n: σὺν ... δέον is tmesis, the preverb standing apart: ‘they bound together’, δέον being the unaugmented imperfect of δέω. θυμαλγέϊ is ‘grieving the heart’, from θυμός and ἄλγος, with δεσμῷ ‘with a bond’. ἀποστρέψαντε is the same dual participle as in 173, and εὖ μάλα is ‘very well’. διαμπερές is ‘right through, thoroughly’. ὡς ἐκέλευσεν is ‘as he ordered’. υἱὸς Λαέρταο has the genitive -αο of the first declension, ‘son of Laertes’, and πολύτλας δῖος Ὀδυσσεύς is a standing name-phrase, ‘much-enduring, heavenly Odysseus’. The ano teleia ends the sentence.

sentences.t:
σειρὴν δὲ πλεκτὴν ἐξ αὐτοῦ πειρήναντε
κίον’ ἀν’ ὑψηλὴν ἔρυσαν πέλασάν τε δοκοῖσι.
sentences.l:
and a plaited rope, from him having fastened it,
up the high pillar they hauled and brought near the beams.
sentences.i: and they fastened a plaited rope to him, hauled him up the high pillar and brought him close to the beams.
sentences.n: This carries out the order of 175–176 almost word for word. The orders were infinitives, ἐρύσαι πελάσαι, and now the deeds are finite past tenses, ἔρυσαν and πέλασαν, ‘they hauled’ and ‘they brought near’; the dative is δοκοῖσι, the form without the final ν. ἐξ αὐτοῦ ‘from him’ is again the rope made fast to the man, as in 175.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἐπικερτομέων προσέφης, Εὔμαιε συβῶτα·
sentences.l: Him, taunting, you addressed, Eumaeus the swineherd:
sentences.i: Taunting him, you said to him, Eumaeus the swineherd:
sentences.n: τὸν is ‘him’, and ἐπικερτομέων is the participle ‘taunting’, from ἐπί and κερτομέω ‘taunt, cut with words’. προσέφης is ‘you addressed’, in the second person: the poet turns to speak to Eumaeus directly, and the name stands in the vocative, Εὔμαιε συβῶτα, ‘Eumaeus the swineherd’. The words he speaks come after the end of this passage.
